clue.text: Pay homage with gold vessel

blocks.note: w is the standard abbreviation for with
or is gold in heraldry
a ship is a seagoing vessel

explanation.surface: Tribute brought to a shrine or ruler in the form of a golden bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' looks like the gold cup being offered; it is a boat. OR for gold comes from heraldry and is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: To worship someone is to revere and honour them, which is exactly what paying homage means.

clue.text: Beat by a tiny margin with no hesitation

indicators.note: 'with no' says the next item is to be left out of what came before

blocks.note: to win by a tiny margin is to win by a whisker
er is the sound of someone hesitating

explanation.surface: A race or contest won by a narrow margin without a moment's pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' reads as defeating a rival; it is the kitchen sense. Dropping ER from the end of WHISKER leaves WHISK.
explanation.definitionFit: To whisk eggs or cream is to beat them rapidly with a utensil, a common cooking synonym.

clue.text: Take away anxiety about holiday, say

indicators.note: 'say' asks for how a word is spoken rather than how it is written

blocks.note: re means about, as in a memo heading
leave is time off work, a holiday

explanation.surface: Someone fretting about a coming trip whose worries need easing.
explanation.walkthrough: RE plus LEAVE, spoken, is exactly how RELIEVE is pronounced; only the spelling of the second half changes.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve someone is to ease or remove their worry, lifting the burden of distress from them.

clue.text: We come out of dwellings with garden tools

indicators.note: something that comes out of a word leaves it, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: we in its object form is us
houses are dwellings

explanation.surface: People emerging from their homes carrying gardening implements.
explanation.walkthrough: Take US out of HOUSES and HOES is left; 'We' has to be turned into its object form first.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoe is a long-handled implement used for weeding and loosening soil in a plot.

clue.text: Officer returned cut diamonds to firm after scam

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so it reads right to left

blocks.note: to lop is to cut off
ice is slang for diamonds
a con is a swindle
firm and stable both mean steady

explanation.surface: A heist story: returned cut diamonds and a fraudulent firm, with an officer on the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut diamonds' looks like one jeweller's phrase, but the words work separately; ice is long-standing slang for diamonds.
explanation.definitionFit: A police constable is the lowest-ranking uniformed officer in the British police force.

clue.text: Started word game with daughter

definitions.note: 'started' in the sense of flinched or was startled

blocks.note: Boggle is a word-finding game played with lettered dice
d is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A family sitting down to begin a word game, a daughter joining in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Started' reads as began; it means gave a start, jumped in surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: To boggle is to hesitate or shy away in alarm, as a horse starts at something frightening.

clue.text: Reportedly purchase tools for fisherman or shepherd in any way you can

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so a spoken word stands for one spelt differently

blocks.note: to purchase is to buy, and it serves before both tools
an angler catches fish on a hook
or stays as it is
a shepherd's hooked staff is a crook

explanation.surface: Shopping for equipment for an angler or a shepherd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' does double duty: buy a hook or buy a crook, each spoken buy spelt BY.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom by hook or by crook means by whatever method is possible, fair or foul.

clue.text: Oversell programme links maybe

blocks.note: read as over plus sell: flog is British slang for sell, and 'over' tells you to turn it
a course is a programme of study or treatment

explanation.surface: Pushing a TV programme too hard, with links to related content.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oversell' looks like one word; split it as over plus sell. Flog is British slang for sell.
explanation.definitionFit: A links is a seaside golf ground, so a links is one example of a place to play golf, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Talk to the French about truce

indicators.note: letters turned about are moved around into a new order

blocks.note: le is French for the
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Negotiating a ceasefire with the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Talk to the French' reads as diplomacy; 'Talk' alone is the definition, and 'the French' supplies LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lecture is a formal speech given to an audience or class, a kind of talk.

clue.text: Absolutely finished with clique

blocks.note: something dead is over and done
a set is a social group or circle

explanation.surface: Someone totally done with a snobbish social group.
explanation.walkthrough: Dead set as an adverb is informal, chiefly Australian and British: 'dead set, mate' means truly.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead set is informal usage for certainly or completely, an emphatic intensifier.

clue.text: The Italian hospital's containing new lethal sickness

indicators.note: to contain is to hold inside, so one piece goes within another
made new, the word's letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: il is Italian for the
h is hospital, as on road signs
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An Italian hospital harbouring a deadly new disease.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's reads as 'has', so the Italian article and the hospital letter together hold the jumbled word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill health is a state of being unwell, a plain synonym for sickness or poor condition.

clue.text: Cleverly craft a piece of material for leotard

indicators.note: a piece is only part of the whole, so the answer is a stretch of the letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Skilfully making a garment for a dancer or gymnast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleverly' reads as an adverb for how to craft; its last two letters start the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycra is a stretchy synthetic fibre used in close-fitting sportswear such as gymnastics costumes.

clue.text: Understood modern pronunciation

indicators.note: pronunciation is how a word is spoken, so we want its sound

blocks.note: modern means new

explanation.surface: Recognising a contemporary way of saying words.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent K means the past tense of know sounds identical to the adjective for modern.
explanation.definitionFit: Knew is the past tense of know, and to have understood something is to have grasped it.

clue.text: Card from best nightspot?

blocks.note: a playing card in the black suit with the trefoil
read as the top one among the dance venues

explanation.surface: A membership or invitation card from the finest club in town.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second reading: ace means best, and a club is a nightspot.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a single playing card, and also whimsically the finest venue among the nightclubs.

clue.text: Cut squeezing of costs in cafe

indicators.note: to squeeze something is to press it inside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: to chop is to cut
of stays as it is
fees are charges or costs

explanation.surface: Trimming expenses at a cafe by squeezing costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squeezing of costs' reads like a budget cut; 'squeezing' is the container signal and 'of' is part of the inserted piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A coffee shop is a small eatery serving drinks and snacks, a close synonym for cafe.

clue.text: Brave woman has stoical heart

indicators.note: the heart of something is its centre, so only central letters are kept

blocks.note: her is the pronoun for a woman
the central three of a seven-letter word

explanation.surface: A courageous woman whose inner nature is stoic.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pulls toward HEROINE for 'brave woman'; 'Brave' alone is the definition and 'woman' is only HER.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic means showing great courage, a direct synonym for brave as an adjective.

clue.text: Get rich fast following work with upper class

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing loosely for the adjective; the defining word is 'rich'

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece goes behind the others

blocks.note: op is opus, a work
U denotes upper class, as in U and non-U speech
Lent is the Christian period of fasting

explanation.surface: Get-rich-quick advice: work hard and mix with posh people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get rich fast' is a stock phrase, but 'fast' is the Lenten fast. U for upper class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulent describes lavish wealth and luxury, being very wealthy and showing it.

clue.text: Reinforce positions backing on to wetland

indicators.note: going backwards, the word reads from right to left

blocks.note: to fit a part is to position it
a fen is low marshy land

explanation.surface: Shoring up defences along the edge of a marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positions' looks like a noun, military posts; it is the verb, as in fits into place.
explanation.definitionFit: To stiffen something is to make it firmer and stronger, which is what reinforcing does.

clue.text: Attempts to raise spirits can fail in religious areas

indicators.note: something that fails falls apart, so its letters are disordered
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
a see is a bishop's diocese

explanation.surface: Efforts to cheer people up falling flat in church districts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise spirits' suggests cheering up; here the spirits are ghosts.
explanation.definitionFit: A seance is a meeting where people try to contact the dead, summoning ghosts through a medium.

clue.text: Plead for troublemaker to have new role

indicators.note: made new, the word's letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: an imp is a mischievous child
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An actor known for mischief begging to be cast in a different part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plead for' reads as one phrase; 'Plead' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore is to beg someone urgently and earnestly, a stronger synonym for pleading.

clue.text: Enjoy the sun and empty excellent hamper

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, a word keeps only its shell

blocks.note: to bask is to lie in warm sunshine
its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A sunny picnic, with a hamper of fine food emptied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamper' could be a verb, to hinder; it is the picnic container.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamper is a large lidded wicker basket, often for picnic food.

clue.text: Deletion of recordings by ’80s' band?

blocks.note: wiping tapes clean
the English synth-pop duo of Vince Clarke and Andy Bell

explanation.surface: A music fan's records by a favourite band from the eighties being wiped.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the pun: a band named for wiping tapes lends its name to the act of wiping them.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasure means wiping out or removing, and it is also the name of a chart-topping pop duo.

clue.text: Sugar worker's cane tipper breaks down

indicators.note: something that breaks down comes apart, so its letters are reassembled

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sugar-plantation worker whose cart for dumping cane has broken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sugar' is not the crop but Alan Sugar, the business magnate who hires contestants on the British TV show The Apprentice.
explanation.definitionFit: The contestants competing for a job with Lord Sugar on the reality show are each called an apprentice.

clue.text: Finishes off last letter with a postscript

blocks.note: z ends the alphabet
a stays as it is
PS is the abbreviation for postscript

explanation.surface: Someone completing a final letter by adding a PS at the bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finishes off last letter' reads as completing correspondence; 'Finishes off' means kills.
explanation.definitionFit: To zap is informal for killing or destroying, especially with a ray gun or sudden blast.

clue.text: Troublesome pest larvae beginning to penetrate wheat

indicators.note: troublesome letters are unruly and will not stay in place
the beginning of a word is its first letter
to penetrate is to go inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
its opening letter

explanation.surface: Grubs of a crop pest boring into a wheat field.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a farming problem; the pest's letters are rearranged around L.
explanation.definitionFit: Spelt is an ancient species of grain related to common bread wheat, used in flour.

clue.text: Keep a journal recording set-up of prank

indicators.note: a recording captures part of what is there, so the answer is inside the words
set up in a down clue means turned to read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run across three words

explanation.surface: A diarist writing down how a practical joke was arranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set-up' looks like the joke's arrangement; in a down clue it sends the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A jape is a practical joke or trick played for fun, a mildly old-fashioned word.

clue.text: Church material?

blocks.note: surface: fabric for vestments or altar hangings
setter's reading: the clergy themselves, known collectively by a word for fabric

explanation.walkthrough: 'Material' reads as fabric bought for the church; it is also the name for people suitable for the church, the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an idiom for the clergy, from clerical dress, and it is also any woven fabric.

clue.text: Hit the roof about Boe's awful review

indicators.note: to review is to go over again, reworking the letters into a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A performer named Boe furious over a scathing critique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' looks like a judgement on the review but is part of the letters; 'review' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are idioms for losing your temper suddenly and explosively in anger.

clue.text: Get soaked putting middle bell back on top of church

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letters
put back, the letters run the other way
putting one piece on another sets them side by side in order

blocks.note: to steep is to soak in liquid
its central two letters

explanation.surface: A bell-ringer getting drenched hauling a bell back up the tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top of church' could be C; it is the definition. A four-letter word has a two-letter middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A steeple is the tall tower and spire rising above a church roof.

clue.text: Most eager to see Kent regenerated

indicators.note: regenerated means formed anew, so the letters are rebuilt in another order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Enthusiasts wanting to visit a revitalised Kent, the English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent is a county in south-east England; 'see' reads as visit but joins it as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Keenest is the superlative of keen, which means enthusiastic, so it is the most enthusiastic.
